headline: The Hidden Cost of AI: Why Saving All That Data Adds Up

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: When you ask an AI to make a video or answer a question, you only see the small result, like a short video clip. But behind the scenes, the computer saves a lot more information than what you see. This includes notes about how it made the answer, backup copies, and safety checks. For one short video, the hidden files were over 100 times bigger than the video itself! All of this extra information has to be stored somewhere, and storing it costs money. Companies often think about the cost of powerful computer chips that run AI, but they forget about the cost of storing all this extra data. As more people use AI every day, this stored data keeps growing and growing. It doesn't go away after the AI finishes its job. Experts say companies need to plan ahead for where all this data will go and how much it will cost, so they don't get surprised by a huge bill later. Planning smart now can save a lot of trouble and money in the future.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: When people use AI to create videos, images, or answers, they usually only notice the final result, like a short video or a quick reply. But creating that small result actually produces a huge amount of extra data behind the scenes. This includes computer logs, backup files, draft versions, and safety records. For example, one short 8-second AI video was less than 4 megabytes, but it left behind over 500 megabytes of hidden data — more than 100 times bigger! Companies often focus on buying powerful computer chips to run AI, since those are expensive and get a lot of attention. But storing all this extra data is also expensive, and it's easy to forget about when planning a budget. Unlike training an AI, which happens once and then stops, using AI (called 'inference') happens every single time someone asks it a question, and it keeps creating new data forever. That data doesn't disappear — it keeps piling up. As more businesses use AI for things like making videos or processing documents, this storage problem grows fast. Experts suggest companies need to think ahead about how they'll store, organize, and reuse all this data, instead of treating storage as an afterthought. They also recommend using cheaper types of storage for data that isn't used very often, while keeping faster storage for things people need right away. Planning this out carefully can help companies avoid unexpected costs that sneak up on them later.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Most conversations about the cost of artificial intelligence focus on the expensive computer chips, called GPUs, that power AI systems. But there's a hidden cost that often gets ignored: data storage. Every time someone uses an AI tool — asking a question, generating an image, or creating a video — the system doesn't just produce the result you see. It also creates a surprising amount of extra data behind the scenes, including activity logs, backup copies, draft versions, and safety records. For example, a company called Western Digital found that one short 8-second AI-generated video, which appeared on-screen as a small 4-megabyte file, actually left behind more than 500 megabytes of hidden data. That's roughly 130 times larger than what the user actually saw. Unlike training an AI model, which is a one-time, limited process companies can budget for, using an already-built AI model (called inference) happens continuously, every time someone uses it. That means data keeps piling up nonstop and never really stops growing. A global survey found that almost all companies using AI have seen their data storage needs increase over the past year, and many have seen it grow by 25% or more. This matters because storage costs can quietly outpace other budgets if companies aren't paying close attention. If a company doesn't plan for this growth, they might save money upfront but get hit with unexpectedly high costs a year or two later. Experts suggest that businesses need a smarter storage strategy — one that uses expensive, fast storage only for information that needs to be accessed instantly, and cheaper, larger storage for information that's used less often but still needs to be kept and occasionally reused for future AI tasks. Companies are now being encouraged to ask themselves important questions, like whether their storage spending would double if their AI usage doubled, and whether they've actually set clear rules for how long to keep AI-generated data. Without good planning, many organizations risk discovering a storage problem only after it has already become expensive and hard to fix.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: When businesses think about the cost of using artificial intelligence, they usually picture expensive computer hardware — specifically GPUs, the specialized chips that process AI tasks. What often gets left out of that picture, though, is the cost of storing data. Every time an AI model responds to a request, it generates far more information than what the user actually sees. This includes system logs, cached data, draft outputs, backup files, and safety compliance records. A real example makes this clear: an AI-generated video that appeared to the user as a small 4-megabyte clip actually left over 500 megabytes of associated data in the background — about 130 times more storage than the visible result. One key reason this problem is so significant is the difference between 'training' an AI model and 'running' it, which is called inference. Training happens in a defined period: a company uses massive computing power for a set amount of time to build or improve a model, and then that process ends. Inference, by contrast, never really stops. Every single time a person interacts with an AI tool, new data is created, and this data tends to stick around rather than being deleted. As AI tools become part of daily business operations — generating marketing videos, processing insurance claims, or powering chatbots — the volume of retained data increases rapidly and shows no signs of slowing down. Industry projections estimate that the demand for running AI models will grow even faster than the demand for training them in the coming years. A global survey of business and technology leaders found that nearly all companies have experienced growing data volumes because of generative AI, with many reporting growth of 25% or more in just one year. This creates a financial risk: while computing costs are relatively predictable and get significant attention from company leadership, storage costs can quietly increase and eventually consume a large portion of an AI program's budget, often without anyone noticing until it's already a serious problem. Experts recommend that organizations rethink their storage strategy entirely, using a mix of storage types: fast, expensive storage for information that needs to be accessed immediately, and larger, more affordable storage for data that accumulates over time but may still be useful later for retrieving information or improving future AI systems. Businesses are encouraged to evaluate their data retention policies, understand whether their storage costs are tied to realistic long-term needs, and estimate whether storage expenses would grow proportionally — or disproportionately — if their AI usage increased. Companies that fail to ask these questions now risk being blindsided by sharply rising costs just as they're trying to decide whether to grow their AI programs further.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Public conversations about the cost of artificial intelligence tend to fixate on one highly visible expense: the specialized computer chips, or GPUs, needed to run AI systems, along with the enormous amounts of electricity they consume. This narrow focus, however, obscures another significant and rapidly growing cost — data storage. Every interaction with an AI system produces far more than the visible output a user receives. Behind each prompt, image, or video lies a trail of system logs, cached context, intermediate computations, backup copies, and compliance or safety records that must be stored, sometimes indefinitely. One striking example illustrates the scale of this issue: an AI-generated video delivered to a user as a 4-megabyte file actually produced over 500 megabytes of associated back-end data — roughly 130 times the size of the visible result. As organizations scale up to generate longer or higher-resolution content, this back-end footprint can balloon into hundreds of gigabytes per piece of content. Central to this problem is a structural difference between two phases of AI deployment: training and inference. Training, the process of building or refining a model, is a finite project with a defined computing cost that organizations can plan and budget for in advance. Inference — the ongoing process of using a trained model to respond to real-world requests — has no such endpoint. Each inference event generates new data, and unlike compute demand, which naturally rises and falls with usage cycles and hardware refresh schedules, the resulting data tends to accumulate rather than disappear. Industry analysts project that demand for inference will grow faster than demand for training over the next several years, eventually accounting for a substantial share of total data center capacity. This trend is already visible: a global survey of IT and business leaders found that the overwhelming majority of organizations have experienced significant increases in data volume linked to generative AI over just the past year, with many reporting growth exceeding 25%. The financial implications are considerable. While compute costs are relatively predictable and receive close scrutiny from organizational leadership, storage costs compound quietly and can eventually represent a disproportionate share of an AI program's total expenses — often becoming apparent only when leadership is evaluating whether to expand the program further. Compounding the challenge, much of this accumulated data is no longer simply archival; it's increasingly treated as a resource to be retrieved and reused for techniques like retrieval-augmented generation, which draws on stored information to improve the accuracy of AI responses. This dual requirement — massive capacity alongside fast, flexible access — demands a more deliberate storage architecture, one that uses expensive, high-performance storage sparingly for truly time-sensitive data while relying on more cost-effective, large-capacity storage solutions for the vast majority of retained information. Ultimately, organizations deploying AI at scale are being urged to examine their data retention policies, assess whether their storage investments reflect the true life cycle of their data rather than short-term training needs, and determine whether their storage costs would scale proportionally — or disproportionately — if AI usage were to double. Failing to answer these questions early risks exposing organizations to escalating costs that undermine the long-term sustainability of their AI initiatives.

questions: If you used an AI tool at school to help with homework or create a project, what kinds of hidden information do you think it might be saving about you without you realizing it?
Why do you think it's easy for people and companies to focus on the flashy parts of new technology (like fast computers) while overlooking less exciting costs like data storage?
If AI use keeps growing in schools, businesses, and everyday life, what kinds of decisions or trade-offs do you think communities will need to make about storing and managing all that extra data?
